claim: Peptidoglycan is the principal constituent of virtually all bacterial surfaces.
source: Peptidoglycan, the principal constituent of virtually all bacterial surfaces, is a specific molecular signature recognized by dedicated host receptors, present in animals and plants, which trigger an immune response.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract without specific citation, drawing on general scientific knowledge about bacterial cell structure.

claim: Peptidoglycan is recognized by dedicated host receptors present in animals and plants.
source: Peptidoglycan, the principal constituent of virtually all bacterial surfaces, is a specific molecular signature recognized by dedicated host receptors, present in animals and plants, which trigger an immune response.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Autolysins from Gram-positive pathogenic bacteria have a major role in concealing peptidoglycan from Drosophila peptidoglycan recognition proteins (PGRPs).
source: Here we report that autolysins from Gram-positive pathogenic bacteria, enzymes capable of hydrolyzing peptidoglycan, have a major role in concealing this inflammatory molecule from Drosophila peptidoglycan recognition proteins (PGRPs).
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experiments shown in the figures.

claim: Autolysins trim the outermost peptidoglycan fragments.
source: We show that autolysins trim the outermost peptidoglycan fragments and that in their absence bacterial virulence is impaired, as PGRPs can directly recognize leftover peptidoglycan extending beyond the external layers of bacterial proteins and polysaccharides.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study supported by experimental data showing PGRP-SA binding to atl mutants.

claim: In the absence of autolysins, bacterial virulence is impaired.
source: We show that autolysins trim the outermost peptidoglycan fragments and that in their absence bacterial virulence is impaired, as PGRPs can directly recognize leftover peptidoglycan extending beyond the external layers of bacterial proteins and polysaccharides.
evidence: This is supported by fly survival experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: PGRPs can directly recognize leftover peptidoglycan extending beyond the external layers of bacterial proteins and polysaccharides when autolysins are absent.
source: We show that autolysins trim the outermost peptidoglycan fragments and that in their absence bacterial virulence is impaired, as PGRPs can directly recognize leftover peptidoglycan extending beyond the external layers of bacterial proteins and polysaccharides.
evidence: This is supported by mCherry_PGRP-SA binding experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: The activity of autolysins is not restricted to the producer cells but can also alter the surface of neighboring bacteria.
source: The activity of autolysins is not restricted to the producer cells but can also alter the surface of neighboring bacteria, facilitating the survival of the entire population in the infected host.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with supernatants shown in Figure 8.

claim: Autolysin activity facilitates the survival of the entire bacterial population in the infected host.
source: The activity of autolysins is not restricted to the producer cells but can also alter the surface of neighboring bacteria, facilitating the survival of the entire population in the infected host.
evidence: This is supported by fly survival experiments with supernatant-treated bacteria shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Peptidoglycan is a macromolecule composed of long glycan strands, cross-linked by short peptides.
source: Peptidoglycan (PGN) is a macromolecule composed of long glycan strands, cross-linked by short peptides, which surrounds most bacterial cells and forms a load-bearing mesh that sustains their shape.
evidence: This is established knowledge about peptidoglycan structure.

claim: Peptidoglycan surrounds most bacterial cells and forms a load-bearing mesh that sustains their shape.
source: Peptidoglycan (PGN) is a macromolecule composed of long glycan strands, cross-linked by short peptides, which surrounds most bacterial cells and forms a load-bearing mesh that sustains their shape.
evidence: This is established knowledge about peptidoglycan function.

claim: Enlargement and remodeling of the PGN mesh during bacterial growth and division requires synthesis of new material catalyzed by penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs).
source: Enlargement and remodeling of the PGN mesh during bacterial growth and division requires not only the synthesis of new material, catalyzed by penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), but also PGN hydrolysis to allow insertion of new material, carried out by PGN autolysins (Vollmer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vollmer et al., 2008.

claim: Enlargement and remodeling of the PGN mesh during bacterial growth and division requires PGN hydrolysis to allow insertion of new material, carried out by PGN autolysins.
source: Enlargement and remodeling of the PGN mesh during bacterial growth and division requires not only the synthesis of new material, catalyzed by penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), but also PGN hydrolysis to allow insertion of new material, carried out by PGN autolysins (Vollmer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vollmer et al., 2008.

claim: Different hosts have specialized receptors that recognize PGN as a pathogen-associated molecular pattern (PAMP) and initiate an inflammatory response to eliminate invading bacteria.
source: Despite its essential role, PGN may also be viewed as an 'Achilles heel' of bacteria during infection, as different hosts have specialized receptors that recognize PGN as a pathogen-associated molecular pattern (PAMP) and initiate an inflammatory response to eliminate invading bacteria.
evidence: This is established knowledge in immunology, supported by subsequent citations.

claim: LysM proteins in plants are receptors that recognize PGN.
source: Examples of these receptors include LysM proteins in plants (Willmann et al., 2011), intracellular NOD-like receptors (NLRs) and Toll-like receptors (TLRs) in mammals (Chaput and Boneca, 2007), and peptidoglycan recognition proteins (PGRPs) in insects and mammals (Dziarski and Gupta, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Willmann et al., 2011.

claim: Intracellular NOD-like receptors (NLRs) and Toll-like receptors (TLRs) in mammals are receptors that recognize PGN.
source: Examples of these receptors include LysM proteins in plants (Willmann et al., 2011), intracellular NOD-like receptors (NLRs) and Toll-like receptors (TLRs) in mammals (Chaput and Boneca, 2007), and peptidoglycan recognition proteins (PGRPs) in insects and mammals (Dziarski and Gupta, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chaput and Boneca, 2007.

claim: Peptidoglycan recognition proteins (PGRPs) in insects and mammals are receptors that recognize PGN.
source: Examples of these receptors include LysM proteins in plants (Willmann et al., 2011), intracellular NOD-like receptors (NLRs) and Toll-like receptors (TLRs) in mammals (Chaput and Boneca, 2007), and peptidoglycan recognition proteins (PGRPs) in insects and mammals (Dziarski and Gupta, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dziarski and Gupta, 2006.

claim: PGRPs were originally isolated due to their high affinity to PGN.
source: PGRPs, originally isolated due to their high affinity to PGN (Kang et al., 1998), are used by Drosophila flies to distinguish between Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, directly at the level of PGN detection.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kang et al., 1998.

claim: PGRPs are used by Drosophila flies to distinguish between Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, directly at the level of PGN detection.
source: PGRPs, originally isolated due to their high affinity to PGN (Kang et al., 1998), are used by Drosophila flies to distinguish between Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, directly at the level of PGN detection.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by subsequent citations.

claim: PGRP-LC specifically recognizes DAP-type PGN, usually found in Gram-negative bacteria and Gram-positive bacilli, and activates the Imd pathway.
source: This is achieved through specific PGRPs: PGRP-LC specifically recognizes DAP-type PGN, usually found in Gram-negative bacteria and Gram-positive bacilli, and activates the Imd pathway (Leulier et al., 2003), while PGRP-SA recognizes lysine-type PGN, which surrounds most Gram-positive bacteria, and activates the Toll pathway (Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Leulier et al., 2003.

claim: PGRP-SA recognizes lysine-type PGN, which surrounds most Gram-positive bacteria, and activates the Toll pathway.
source: This is achieved through specific PGRPs: PGRP-LC specifically recognizes DAP-type PGN, usually found in Gram-negative bacteria and Gram-positive bacilli, and activates the Imd pathway (Leulier et al., 2003), while PGRP-SA recognizes lysine-type PGN, which surrounds most Gram-positive bacteria, and activates the Toll pathway (Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007.

claim: Activation of either the Imd or Toll pathway results in a series of multiple defense reactions that include the production and secretion of antimicrobial peptides into the hemolymph of flies.
source: Activation of either pathway results in a series of multiple defense reactions that include the production and secretion of antimicrobial peptides into the hemolymph of flies (Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007.

claim: In mammals, PGRPs can act as antibacterial agents due to their bactericidal and/or bacteriostatic activity.
source: In mammals, PGRPs can act as antibacterial agents due to their bactericidal and/or bacteriostatic activity, mediated by PGN hydrolytic activity (e.g. PGLYRP-2 [Dziarski and Gupta, 2006]) or by the binding of PGRPs to targets on the bacterial cell surface, which causes the activation of specific bacterial two-component systems, resulting in bacteria killing through a mechanism that includes membrane depolarization and production of hydroxyl radicals (Kashyap et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dziarski and Gupta, 2006 and Kashyap et al., 2011.

claim: Mammalian PGRP antibacterial activity can be mediated by PGN hydrolytic activity.
source: In mammals, PGRPs can act as antibacterial agents due to their bactericidal and/or bacteriostatic activity, mediated by PGN hydrolytic activity (e.g. PGLYRP-2 [Dziarski and Gupta, 2006]) or by the binding of PGRPs to targets on the bacterial cell surface, which causes the activation of specific bacterial two-component systems, resulting in bacteria killing through a mechanism that includes membrane depolarization and production of hydroxyl radicals (Kashyap et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dziarski and Gupta, 2006.

claim: Mammalian PGRP antibacterial activity can be mediated by binding of PGRPs to targets on the bacterial cell surface, which causes the activation of specific bacterial two-component systems, resulting in bacteria killing through membrane depolarization and production of hydroxyl radicals.
source: In mammals, PGRPs can act as antibacterial agents due to their bactericidal and/or bacteriostatic activity, mediated by PGN hydrolytic activity (e.g. PGLYRP-2 [Dziarski and Gupta, 2006]) or by the binding of PGRPs to targets on the bacterial cell surface, which causes the activation of specific bacterial two-component systems, resulting in bacteria killing through a mechanism that includes membrane depolarization and production of hydroxyl radicals (Kashyap et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kashyap et al., 2011.

claim: Bacterial PGN is concealed by an outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria.
source: Bacterial PGN is concealed by an outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria, or by layers of proteins and glycopolymers in Gram-positive bacteria.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial cell structure.

claim: Bacterial PGN is concealed by layers of proteins and glycopolymers in Gram-positive bacteria.
source: Bacterial PGN is concealed by an outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria, or by layers of proteins and glycopolymers in Gram-positive bacteria.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial cell structure.

claim: It is usually assumed that an infected organism only recognizes PGN in the form of fragments released into the surrounding medium by the activity of different bacterial or host enzymes.
source: It is therefore usually assumed that an infected organism only recognizes PGN in the form of fragments released into the surrounding medium by the activity of different bacterial or host enzymes (Nigro et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nigro et al., 2008.

claim: PGRP-SA can directly bind PGN at the bacterial surface in conditions such as the absence of wall teichoic acids (WTAs).
source: However, it has been recently shown that PGRP-SA can directly bind PGN at the bacterial surface in conditions such as the absence of wall teichoic acids (WTAs) (Atilano et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Atilano et al., 2011.

claim: A mutant lacking the major autolysin Atl was identified as the most severely impaired in its ability to avoid recognition by mCherry_PGRP-SA.
source: A mutant lacking the major autolysin Atl, a PGN hydrolase, was identified as the most severely impaired in its ability to avoid recognition by mCherry_PGRP-SA.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: An S. aureus atl null mutant produces a PGN with a muropeptide composition similar to the parental strain.
source: However, an S. aureus atl null mutant produces a PGN with a muropeptide composition similar to the parental strain (Figure 2A), that is, it shows no increase in the amount of polymerized muropeptides, which were previously reported to be better inducers of an innate immune response than monomeric muropeptides (Filipe et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 2A and cited work by Filipe et al., 2005.

claim: The S. aureus atl null mutant shows no increase in the amount of polymerized muropeptides.
source: However, an S. aureus atl null mutant produces a PGN with a muropeptide composition similar to the parental strain (Figure 2A), that is, it shows no increase in the amount of polymerized muropeptides, which were previously reported to be better inducers of an innate immune response than monomeric muropeptides (Filipe et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Polymerized muropeptides were previously reported to be better inducers of an innate immune response than monomeric muropeptides.
source: However, an S. aureus atl null mutant produces a PGN with a muropeptide composition similar to the parental strain (Figure 2A), that is, it shows no increase in the amount of polymerized muropeptides, which were previously reported to be better inducers of an innate immune response than monomeric muropeptides (Filipe et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Filipe et al., 2005.

claim: The S. aureus atl null mutant produces WTAs.
source: Moreover, the S. aureus atl null mutant produces WTAs (Figure 2B), indicating that the mechanism to conceal PGN dependent on the presence of atl is new, and different from that previously reported for a WTA mutant (Atilano et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by PAGE analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The mechanism to conceal PGN dependent on the presence of atl is new, and different from that previously reported for a WTA mutant.
source: Moreover, the S. aureus atl null mutant produces WTAs (Figure 2B), indicating that the mechanism to conceal PGN dependent on the presence of atl is new, and different from that previously reported for a WTA mutant (Atilano et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data in Figure 2B and comparison to previous work cited as Atilano et al., 2011.

claim: The simultaneous deletion of tagO and atl had a synergistic effect on exposing the surface PGN to host recognition.
source: In agreement, the simultaneous deletion of tagO and atl had a synergistic effect on exposing the surface PGN to host recognition (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The atl gene encodes a polypeptide that is cleaved into two proteins capable of digesting PGN: an amidase (AM) and a glucosaminidase (GL).
source: The atl gene encodes a polypeptide that is cleaved into two proteins capable of digesting PGN: an amidase (AM), which cleaves the amide bond between peptides and glycans, and a glucosaminidase (GL), which cleaves glycan strands (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Atl structure and is illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: The amidase (AM) cleaves the amide bond between peptides and glycans.
source: The atl gene encodes a polypeptide that is cleaved into two proteins capable of digesting PGN: an amidase (AM), which cleaves the amide bond between peptides and glycans, and a glucosaminidase (GL), which cleaves glycan strands (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about amidase activity and is illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: The glucosaminidase (GL) cleaves glycan strands.
source: The atl gene encodes a polypeptide that is cleaved into two proteins capable of digesting PGN: an amidase (AM), which cleaves the amide bond between peptides and glycans, and a glucosaminidase (GL), which cleaves glycan strands (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about glucosaminidase activity and is illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: Either amidase or glucosaminidase enzymatic activity was sufficient to impair recognition of S. aureus by PGRP-SA.
source: When the atl mutants were incubated with mCherry-PGRP-SA, both the mutant having only glucosaminidase activity (AMH265A mutant) and the mutant having only amidase activity (GLE1128A mutant) were still able to avoid strong PGRP-SA binding, indicating that either amidase or glucosaminidase enzymatic activity was sufficient to impair recognition of S. aureus by PGRP-SA (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Only when both amidase and glucosaminidase activities were absent was mCherry-PGRP-SA capable of easily recognizing the bacterial cell surface.
source: Only when both activities were absent (AtlH265A/E1128A double mutant) was mCherry-PGRP-SA capable of easily recognizing the bacterial cell surface (Figure 3C,D), albeit to lower levels than those observed for the atl null mutant.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: The difference in PGRP-SA recognition between the AtlH265A/E1128A double mutant and the atl null mutant may be due to residual amidase or glucosaminidase activity in the double mutant, not detectable in a zymogram.
source: This difference may be due to residual amidase or glucosaminidase activity in the S. aureus AtlH265A/E1128A double mutant, not detectable in a zymogram.
evidence: This is speculation to explain the observed difference in data.

claim: Pre-incubation of S. aureus atl null mutant cells with either AM or GL completely abolished mCherry_PGRP-SA binding to the bacterial surface.
source: Pre-incubation of S. aureus atl null mutant cells with either AM or GL (approximately 0.4 μM) completely abolished mCherry_PGRP-SA binding to the bacterial surface (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: When both AM and GL enzymes were added simultaneously to the atl null mutant cells, lower concentrations of each enzyme were sufficient to conceal bacteria from the host immune receptor.
source: When both enzymes were added simultaneously to the atl null mutant cells, lower concentrations of each enzyme (<0.02 μM) were sufficient to conceal bacteria from the host immune receptor (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The synergy in PGRP-SA binding observed for the S. aureus AtlH265A/E1128 double mutant is in agreement with the synergistic effect of combining AM and GL enzymes.
source: This is in agreement with the synergy in PGRP-SA binding observed for the S. aureus AtlH265A/E1128 double mutant (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the data from Figure 4B with Figure 2C.

claim: The activity of the autolysins, and not their physical presence, was required for protection from PGRP-SA recognition.
source: This procedure did not increase recognition by PGRP-SA, showing that the activity of the autolysins, and not their physical presence, was required for protection.
evidence: This is supported by the washing experiment shown in Figure 5.

claim: S. aureus atl mutants are impaired in their virulence.
source: Indeed, Tabuchi et al. have previously shown that S. aureus atl mutants are impaired in their virulence (Tabuchi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tabuchi et al., 2010.

claim: The atl mutant used in this work, when compared to the parental S. aureus strain NCTC8325-4, was severely impaired in its ability to kill wild type Drosophila.
source: We have confirmed that the atl mutant used in this work, when compared to the parental S. aureus strain NCTC8325-4, was also severely impaired in its ability to kill wild type Drosophila, both the 25174 strain, recently established from wild caught flies (Mackay et al., 2012), as well as the yw strain, which is the parental lineage used to generate the PGRP seml mutant (Michel et al., 2001; Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is supported by fly survival data shown in Figure 6A and 6B, and citations to Mackay et al., 2012 and Michel et al., 2001.

claim: The atl mutant triggered a stronger induction of drosomycin expression when normalized for the same number of infecting bacteria.
source: Furthermore, the atl mutant triggered a stronger induction of drosomycin expression (frequently used as a read-out for Toll activity) when normalized for the same number of infecting bacteria (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Survival of Drosophila infected with an S. aureus atl mutant was dependent upon the presence of a functional PGRP-SA.
source: Importantly, our data showed that survival of Drosophila infected with an S. aureus atl mutant was dependent upon the presence of a functional PGRP-SA (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by fly survival data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The atl mutant bacteria were capable of propagating similarly to the parental S. aureus strain in flies that lacked a functional PGRP-SA.
source: Furthermore, these mutant bacteria were capable of propagating similarly to the parental S. aureus strain in flies that lacked a functional PGRP-SA (Figure 6F), showing that impaired virulence is not due to a lower proliferation rate of the atl mutant.
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Impaired virulence of the atl mutant is not due to a lower proliferation rate of the atl mutant.
source: Furthermore, these mutant bacteria were capable of propagating similarly to the parental S. aureus strain in flies that lacked a functional PGRP-SA (Figure 6F), showing that impaired virulence is not due to a lower proliferation rate of the atl mutant.
evidence: This is an inference based on the CFU data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Inactivation of either the amidase or the glucosaminidase activity resulted in decreased virulence.
source: We therefore tested the virulence of bacteria with either impaired amidase activity (AMH265A) or impaired glucosaminidase activity (GLE1128A) and observed that both had a reduced ability to kill flies (Figure 7A) in accordance with the second hypothesis.
evidence: This is supported by fly survival data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Injection of seml Drosophila with atl mutant bacteria pre-coated with mCherry_PGRP-SA resulted in increased fly survival.
source: Moreover, injection of seml Drosophila with atl mutant bacteria pre-coated with mCherry_PGRP-SA resulted in increased fly survival (Figure 7B), again favoring a role for PGRP-SA in the recognition of PGN directly at the bacterial surface.
evidence: This is supported by fly survival data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: A continuous and high expression of PGRP-SA during the entire infection process is required to ensure survival of the infected host.
source: This is in accordance with the hypothesis that a continuous and high expression of PGRP-SA during the entire infection process is required to ensure survival of the infected host (De Gregorio et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to De Gregorio et al., 2001.

claim: Secreted autolysins can bind to bacterial cell surfaces and can also be found in the growth medium.
source: Secreted autolysins not only bind to bacterial cell surfaces but they can also be found in the growth medium (Pasztor et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pasztor et al., 2010.

claim: The atl-encoded proteins secreted into the supernatant by the parental strain were capable of modifying the surface of the atl null mutant cells, consequently abolishing their recognition by PGRP-SA.
source: The atl-encoded proteins secreted into the supernatant by the parental strain were capable of modifying the surface of the atl null mutant cells, consequently abolishing their recognition by PGRP-SA (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8A and 8B.

claim: Supernatant from a culture of S. aureus atl null mutant did not abolish PGRP-SA recognition of atl null mutant cells.
source: This was not observed when supernatant from a culture of S. aureus atl null mutant was used (Figure 8A,B), showing that atl products (and not other secreted PGN hydrolases) are responsible for PGN concealment.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8A and 8B.

claim: Atl products (and not other secreted PGN hydrolases) are responsible for PGN concealment.
source: This was not observed when supernatant from a culture of S. aureus atl null mutant was used (Figure 8A,B), showing that atl products (and not other secreted PGN hydrolases) are responsible for PGN concealment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of supernatants shown in Figure 8A and 8B.

claim: Atl mutants regained the ability to kill flies if pre-treated with a supernatant from a culture of the Atl producer NCTC8325-4 but not if pre-treated with supernatant from a culture of the atl mutant.
source: Importantly, we observed that atl mutants regained the ability to kill flies if pre-treated with a supernatant from a culture of the Atl producer NCTC8325-4 but not if pre-treated with supernatant from a culture of the atl mutant (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by fly survival data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Previously bound PGRP-SA could be removed by autolysin activity present in the medium.
source: Moreover, previously bound PGRP-SA could be removed by autolysin activity present in the medium, as seen by time-lapse microscopy of S. aureus atl null mutant cells initially covered by bound mCherry_PGRP-SA and then incubated with supernatant containing amidase and glucosaminidase enzymes (Figure 9).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The autolysins encoded by atl can protect not only the producer cells but also a population of invading bacteria from detection by the immune system during infection.
source: Together, these data suggest that the autolysins encoded by atl can protect not only the producer cells but also a population of invading bacteria from detection by the immune system during infection, enabling it to kill the infected host.
evidence: This is an inference based on the supernatant experiments shown in Figures 8 and 9.

claim: Deletion of the atl gene in MW2 led to higher binding of mCherry_PGRP-SA.
source: Deletion of the atl gene in MW2 led to higher binding of mCherry_PGRP-SA, that is, to improved recognition of the bacterial surface (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: MW2Δatl cells were severely impaired in virulence, as demonstrated by the decreased capacity to kill Drosophila.
source: More importantly, MW2Δatl cells were severely impaired in virulence, as demonstrated by the decreased capacity to kill Drosophila (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is supported by fly survival data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: Lack of LytA, the major amidase of S. pneumoniae, resulted in bacteria that were better recognized by mCherry_PGRP-SA.
source: Lack of LytA, the major amidase of S. pneumoniae, resulted in bacteria that were better recognized by mCherry_PGRP-SA, a phenotype that was reversed when LytA was expressed from a plasmid (Figure 11A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 11A.

claim: Expression of LytA from a plasmid reversed the increased PGRP-SA recognition phenotype of the lytA mutant.
source: Lack of LytA, the major amidase of S. pneumoniae, resulted in bacteria that were better recognized by mCherry_PGRP-SA, a phenotype that was reversed when LytA was expressed from a plasmid (Figure 11A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 11A.

claim: S. pneumoniae LytA and Streptomyces globisporus mutanolysin were capable of protecting S. aureus atl null mutant cells from PGRP-SA recognition.
source: Interestingly, it is possible that autolysins can participate in inter-species protection, as S. pneumoniae LytA, an amidase that releases PGN stem peptides, and Streptomyces globisporus mutanolysin, a commercially available muramidase that releases muropeptides, were capable of protecting S. aureus atl null mutant cells from PGRP-SA recognition (Figure 11B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 11B.

claim: Autolysins can participate in inter-species protection.
source: Interestingly, it is possible that autolysins can participate in inter-species protection, as S. pneumoniae LytA, an amidase that releases PGN stem peptides, and Streptomyces globisporus mutanolysin, a commercially available muramidase that releases muropeptides, were capable of protecting S. aureus atl null mutant cells from PGRP-SA recognition (Figure 11B).
evidence: This is speculation based on the data shown in Figure 11B.

claim: Bacteria have evolved various independent mechanisms to prevent direct recognition by PGN host receptors.
source: We propose that bacteria have evolved various independent mechanisms to prevent direct recognition by PGN host receptors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in the study.

claim: The presence of glycopolymers, such as WTAs, at the bacterial surface contributes to S. aureus evasion from the Drosophila innate immune system.
source: We have previously shown that the presence of glycopolymers, such as WTAs, at the bacterial surface contributes to S. aureus evasion from the Drosophila innate immune system (Atilano et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Atilano et al., 2011.

claim: Atl protects bacteria from host recognition by a different mechanism than WTAs.
source: We now show that Atl also protects bacteria from host recognition but by a different mechanism, given that simultaneous deletion of tagO (essential for teichoic acid biosynthesis) and atl had a synergistic effect on exposing the surface PGN to host recognition, when compared to individual deletion of each of these genes, as shown in Figure 2C.
evidence: This is an inference based on the synergistic effect shown in Figure 2C.

claim: This new role for Atl is in accordance with previous reports that have shown in the Drosophila infection model that S. aureus atl mutants are impaired in their virulence.
source: This new role for Atl is in accordance with previous reports that have shown in the Drosophila infection model that S. aureus atl mutants are impaired in their virulence (Tabuchi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tabuchi et al., 2010.

claim: Bacterial autolysins, or murein hydrolases, are present in most bacteria.
source: Bacterial autolysins, or murein hydrolases, are present in most bacteria and have been recognized as important players in bacterial metabolism.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial autolysins.

claim: Autolysins are required to cleave the pre-existing PGN structure so that new PGN subunits are incorporated during synthesis.
source: Autolysins are required, among other roles, to cleave the pre-existing PGN structure so that new PGN subunits are incorporated during synthesis, to ensure daughter cell separation after complete bacterial division or to prompt antibiotic-induced lysis of bacterial cells (Vollmer et al., 2008; Uehara and Bernhardt, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vollmer et al., 2008 and Uehara and Bernhardt, 2011.

claim: Autolysins are required to ensure daughter cell separation after complete bacterial division.
source: Autolysins are required, among other roles, to cleave the pre-existing PGN structure so that new PGN subunits are incorporated during synthesis, to ensure daughter cell separation after complete bacterial division or to prompt antibiotic-induced lysis of bacterial cells (Vollmer et al., 2008; Uehara and Bernhardt, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vollmer et al., 2008 and Uehara and Bernhardt, 2011.

claim: Autolysins are required to prompt antibiotic-induced lysis of bacterial cells.
source: Autolysins are required, among other roles, to cleave the pre-existing PGN structure so that new PGN subunits are incorporated during synthesis, to ensure daughter cell separation after complete bacterial division or to prompt antibiotic-induced lysis of bacterial cells (Vollmer et al., 2008; Uehara and Bernhardt, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vollmer et al., 2008 and Uehara and Bernhardt, 2011.

claim: Autolysins have been recognized as important virulence factors, as they may act as adhesins.
source: Autolysins have also been recognized as important virulence factors, as they may act as adhesins (Hell et al., 1998) or be required for biofilm formation (Vollmer et al., 2008; Uehara and Bernhardt, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hell et al., 1998.

claim: Autolysins may be required for biofilm formation.
